stories.title: Chinese humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games
stories.summary:
Chinese humanoid robots broke human records in the 100-meter sprint and high jump during the opening day of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing.

The event, described as an Olympics-like competition for robotics, featured a Chinese robot completing the 100m dash in 9.39 seconds. This performance surpassed Usain Bolt’s long-standing human world record of 9.58 seconds.

Multiple international outlets, including Al Jazeera and the BBC, reported on the milestone, highlighting the rapid advancement of humanoid robotics in athletic performance.

stories.title: Tropical Storm Moke advances toward Hawaii as winds strengthen
stories.summary:
Tropical Storm Moke advanced toward Hawaii on Saturday, bringing the threat of heavy rainfall and strong gusts to the Big Island. The storm is expected to intensify as it approaches the island.

Residents are already dealing with the aftermath of Hurricane Lala, which caused significant flooding and damaging winds earlier in the week. This marks the second consecutive week that Hawaii Island has faced threats from an intensifying tropical system.

stories.title: Swedish police identify 17-year-old girl as victim in school sword attack
stories.summary:
Swedish police have identified the victim of a deadly sword attack at Brinell School as a 17-year-old girl. The incident occurred on Friday and resulted in one fatality.

The school's principal confirmed that the 18-year-old suspect detained by authorities was a student at the institution. Police reports indicate that two other students, boys aged 12 and 17, were also injured during the attack.

stories.title: Federal judge strikes down State Department visa ban on 75 countries
stories.summary:
A federal judge in New York has struck down a State Department policy that suspended immigrant visa processing for applicants from 75 countries. The ruling, issued by U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, determined that Secretary of State Marco Rubio lacked the authority to order such denials.

The policy was implemented in January and targeted applicants who had already been found eligible for visas. In a 61-page decision, Judge Vargas described the administration's approach as contrary to established legal standards.

Fox News characterized the judge's ruling as a rebuke of what it called an "Orwellian" freeze on visa processing. The decision effectively halts the suspension of immigrant visa services for the affected nations.

stories.title: Fur seal’s death marks first Australian mainland mammal fatality from spreading H5 bird flu strain
stories.summary:
A long-nosed fur seal found dead at Beachport in South Australia has tested positive for the H5 bird flu strain. This marks the first confirmed mainland mammal fatality from the virus in Australia.

The discovery has prompted warnings from government officials about potential significant losses to wildlife and agriculture. The case highlights the expanding reach of the spreading avian influenza strain beyond birds into other animal populations.

stories.title: I’d heard ringing in my ears before. This time, it didn’t stop
stories.summary:
Miranda Luby was 36 when she experienced a sudden onset of tinnitus one night two years ago. The high-pitched electronic hum began without warning while she was in bed.

Luby initially believed the sound was coming from an external source and spent about half an hour checking various electrical appliances around her house. She eventually realized the ringing was originating inside her own head.

The experience was described as traumatic, marking a significant change from previous instances of temporary ear ringing.

stories.summary:
Timothy Garton Ash argues that even a catastrophic AI failure on the scale of Hiroshima may not be enough to force humanity to protect itself. Writing from Silicon Valley, he describes an environment where experts expect an extraordinary takeoff in artificial intelligence within the next couple of years.

The piece frames the coming breakthrough as “recursive self-improvement,” a point at which AI systems begin improving themselves faster than humans can intervene. Garton Ash suggests that this acceleration is outpacing humanity’s ability to control it, making even sober predictions seem optimistic.
